# InventoryRepository.kt

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt](../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-24

## Role

The data-access layer for inventory, written by Robert. It is the only class that talks to the
`inventory` table (created by [V1__create_inventory.sql](../resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md)).
Request flow for `GET /inventory`: controller → service → **repository** → Postgres. Each row
comes back as an `InventoryItem`. [InventoryRepositoryTest](../../test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)
checks it against a real Postgres.

Robert's own summary, written while he worked on it:

> The class initializes the JDBC client, which allows us to make SQL queries. `findAll` has the
> return type `List<InventoryItem>`: we query the database for all entries and order them
> alphabetically by `sku_id`. We are explicit in the query with the result-set lambda so that
> Kotlin knows we are getting inventory items and each item is non-null. Otherwise Kotlin won't
> compile, because we haven't dealt with the null case.

## Walkthrough

### Imports

```kotlin
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository
```

**Kotlin:** Kotlin imports `kotlin.*` automatically (like Java's `java.lang`), and classes in the
same package need no import, which is why `InventoryItem` has none. Everything from a library,
Spring included, has to be imported.

### A Spring bean with constructor injection

```kotlin
/** Reads inventory rows from Postgres, used by the service layer. */
@Repository
class InventoryRepository(
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
){
```

**Kotlin:** the parentheses after the class name are the **primary constructor**. `private val`
in front of a parameter declares a property and assigns it in one step. The Java equivalent is a
`private final JdbcClient jdbcClient;` field plus a constructor that sets it. `private` because
nothing outside the repository should reach into its database handle. `val` because the reference
never changes.

The **trailing comma** after the last parameter is optional. Kotlin style recommends it when each
item sits on its own line: adding a second parameter later then changes one line in the diff
instead of two, and lines can be reordered without fixing commas. Java allows this in array
initializers but not in parameter lists.

**Kotlin (KDoc):** `/** ... */` is **KDoc**, Kotlin's Javadoc. It belongs to the declaration
*directly* below it (annotations may sit in between, but a blank line or another comment
detaches it). The editor shows it when you hover over the class or function anywhere in the
project. It answers "what does this do?" for the caller. A `// Why:` comment answers "why is it
built this way?" for whoever changes the file, and the editor ignores it. The project's
[check_kdoc.py](../../../../../scripts/check_kdoc.py) requires KDoc on every non-private declaration.

**Spring:** two separate things happen here.
1. **Bean creation.** At startup, `@SpringBootApplication` scans its package and every package
   below it for classes with a stereotype annotation: `@Component`, or one of its specialized
   forms, `@Repository`, `@Service` and `@RestController`. `@Repository` is what makes Spring create
   an `InventoryRepository` in the running app. Without it, the service can't be injected, and the
   app fails to start with `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`. The test doesn't need the annotation,
   because `@Import(InventoryRepository::class)` registers the class by hand. That's why the test
   alone can't prove the annotation is there. The full-context controller test does.
   `@Repository` rather than a plain `@Component` because it names the class's role: data access.
2. **Constructor injection.** Spring sees that the class has a single constructor, and fills in its
   parameters with matching beans. No `@Autowired` is needed for a single constructor. The test
   class needs `@Autowired` because JUnit creates it, not Spring. The `JdbcClient` bean itself
   comes from Spring Boot's auto-configuration, which builds a `DataSource` from the datasource
   settings and a `JdbcClient` on top of it. Beans are created at startup, so a missing dependency
   fails fast instead of on the first request.

**Spring (exception translation):** `JdbcClient` already turns `SQLException`s into Spring's
`DataAccessException` hierarchy (see the backstop test's `DataIntegrityViolationException`).
For JDBC code, `@Repository` is mostly about bean creation and naming the role.

### `findAll`: the function signature

```kotlin
/** Returns every SKU with its quantity, sorted by SKU id; zero-stock SKUs included, empty list when none. */
fun findAll(): List<InventoryItem> = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory ORDER BY sku_id")
```

**Kotlin:** a function is `fun name(params): ReturnType`. Parameters are written `name: Type`,
the reverse of Java, and the return type comes after the parentheses. `findAll` takes no
parameters. No modifier means `public`, which is what the service needs
([public by default](../../test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)).

`List<InventoryItem>` is a generic type, as in Java. Two Kotlin differences:
- **`List` is read-only.** It has no `add` or `remove`. A changeable list is a `MutableList`. The
  caller gets a snapshot it can't modify.
- **No `?`, so never null.** The compiler won't let this function return `null`. That's how the
  "empty list, never null" test is guaranteed by the type, not just by the implementation.

**Kotlin (expression body):** `= expression` instead of `{ ... return ... }`. The whole body is one
call chain, so its result is the return value. Robert first wrote a block body with a local `val`
and `return`, and shortened it once it passed. Concept explained in full in
[TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean).

**SQL:**
- `SELECT sku_id, quantity` names the columns instead of `SELECT *`. The row mapper below reads
  those two columns by name, so the query states exactly what the mapper depends on. A column
  added later can't silently change what the query returns.
- `ORDER BY sku_id`: without `ORDER BY`, SQL guarantees **no** order. Postgres returns rows in
  whatever order is cheapest, which can change after updates, deletes or a new query plan. The
  decision (2026-09-24) was to sort by SKU id so every response is deterministic. `sku_id` is
  `TEXT`, so the order is alphabetical, not numeric. The test inserts SKUs out of order to prove it.
- Column names are the **database** names (`sku_id`, snake_case), not the Kotlin property
  names (`skuId`).

**Spring:** `jdbcClient.sql(...)` only *prepares* a statement. Nothing runs until a terminal
call such as `.list()`.

### Mapping each row: the lambda

```kotlin
// Why: Chose the result set lambda instead of InventoryItem::class.java so Kotlin sees the items as non null.
        .query { rs, _ ->
            InventoryItem(rs.getString("sku_id"), rs.getInt("quantity"))
        }
        .list()
```

**Kotlin (lambdas):** `{ rs, _ -> ... }` is a **lambda**, a function written inline. Parameters go
left of `->` and the result goes right. The last expression is the return value, with no `return`.
- `rs` is only a name (short for `ResultSet`, the JDBC convention). `row` would work just as well.
- `_` means "there's a parameter here, and I don't use it". Spring's `RowMapper` always passes
  two arguments (the result set and the row number), so the lambda must accept two.
- The types are inferred from `RowMapper`, so you never write `rs: ResultSet`.
- **Trailing lambda:** when a lambda is the last argument, it moves outside the parentheses, and
  when it's the only one, the parentheses disappear, so `.query { ... }` instead of `.query({ ... })`.
  See [trailing lambdas](../../build.gradle.kts.md#the-file-is-kotlin-trailing-lambdas).
- **SAM conversion:** `RowMapper` is a Java interface with a single abstract method. Kotlin lets a
  lambda stand in for it. In Java you'd write the lambda `(rs, rowNum) -> new InventoryItem(...)`.

**JDBC:** `rs.getString("sku_id")` and `rs.getInt("quantity")` read the current row's columns by
database name. Every name here must appear in the `SELECT`, or it fails at runtime with "column
not found". Reading by position (`getInt(2)`) also works, but breaks silently if the `SELECT` is
reordered.

**Why a hand-written lambda and not `query(InventoryItem::class.java)`:** Robert's first version
used the class-based mapping, and it didn't compile:

```
Return type mismatch: expected 'List<InventoryItem>', actual '(Mutable)List<InventoryItem?>'.
```

Spring 7 annotates its Java API with JSpecify nullability annotations, and Kotlin reads them
(see [platform types](../../build.gradle.kts.md#compiler-options)). In spring-jdbc 7.0.9:

```java
<T> MappedQuerySpec<@Nullable T> query(Class<T> mappedClass);
<T extends @Nullable Object> MappedQuerySpec<T> query(RowMapper<T> rowMapper);
```

- The class-based version is declared as "each row *might* map to null", because it also handles
  single-column queries where the value can be SQL `NULL`. So Kotlin sees `InventoryItem?`.
- The row-mapper version keeps the lambda's own return type. The lambda always builds a real
  `InventoryItem`, so the list is `List<InventoryItem>`.

The fix works at **compile time**: the class-based mapping would never actually have returned null
for these rows, but the compiler couldn't prove it. It's also more explicit, since you can see
which column goes into which property. That fits the reason `JdbcClient` was chosen (explicit SQL).

`(Mutable)List` is Kotlin saying it can't tell whether a Java `List` is meant to be changed. It's
harmless, because it fits a read-only `List` return type.

**Null safety, one level deeper:** `rs.getString(...)` is a Java method, so its result is a
platform type (`String!`). If it were ever null, Kotlin would throw when passing it into
`InventoryItem`'s non-null `skuId`. That can't happen: `sku_id` is the primary key, and a primary
key is never NULL. The migration's constraints back up the Kotlin types.

**Spring:** `.list()` runs the query, calls the lambda once per row, and collects the results. No
rows means an empty list, never null.

## Role

The data-access layer for inventory, written by Robert. It is the only class that talks to the
`inventory` table (created by [V1__create_inventory.sql](../resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md)).
Request flow for `GET /inventory`: controller → service → **repository** → Postgres. Each row
comes back as an `InventoryItem`. [InventoryRepositoryTest](../../test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)
checks it against a real Postgres.

Robert's own summary, written while he worked on it:

> The class initializes the JDBC client, which allows us to make SQL queries. `findAll` has the
> return type `List<InventoryItem>`: we query the database for all entries and order them
> alphabetically by `sku_id`. We are explicit in the query with the result-set lambda so that
> Kotlin knows we are getting inventory items and each item is non-null. Otherwise Kotlin won't
> compile, because we haven't dealt with the null case.

## Walkthrough

### Imports

```kotlin
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository
```

**Kotlin:** Kotlin imports `kotlin.*` automatically (like Java's `java.lang`), and classes in the
same package need no import, which is why `InventoryItem` has none. Everything from a library,
Spring included, has to be imported.

### A Spring bean with constructor injection

```kotlin
/** Reads inventory rows from Postgres, used by the service layer. */
@Repository
class InventoryRepository(
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
){
```

**Kotlin:** the parentheses after the class name are the **primary constructor**. `private val`
in front of a parameter declares a property and assigns it in one step. The Java equivalent is a
`private final JdbcClient jdbcClient;` field plus a constructor that sets it. `private` because
nothing outside the repository should reach into its database handle. `val` because the reference
never changes.

The **trailing comma** after the last parameter is optional. Kotlin style recommends it when each
item sits on its own line: adding a second parameter later then changes one line in the diff
instead of two, and lines can be reordered without fixing commas. Java allows this in array
initializers but not in parameter lists.

**Kotlin (KDoc):** `/** ... */` is **KDoc**, Kotlin's Javadoc. It belongs to the declaration
*directly* below it (annotations may sit in between, but a blank line or another comment
detaches it). The editor shows it when you hover over the class or function anywhere in the
project. It answers "what does this do?" for the caller. A `// Why:` comment answers "why is it
built this way?" for whoever changes the file, and the editor ignores it. The project's
[check_kdoc.py](../../../../../scripts/check_kdoc.py) requires KDoc on every non-private declaration.

**Spring:** two separate things happen here.
1. **Bean creation.** At startup, `@SpringBootApplication` scans its package and every package
   below it for classes with a stereotype annotation: `@Component`, or one of its specialized
   forms, `@Repository`, `@Service` and `@RestController`. `@Repository` is what makes Spring create
   an `InventoryRepository` in the running app. Without it, the service can't be injected, and the
   app fails to start with `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`. The test doesn't need the annotation,
   because `@Import(InventoryRepository::class)` registers the class by hand. That's why the test
   alone can't prove the annotation is there. The full-context controller test does.
   `@Repository` rather than a plain `@Component` because it names the class's role: data access.
2. **Constructor injection.** Spring sees that the class has a single constructor, and fills in its
   parameters with matching beans. No `@Autowired` is needed for a single constructor. The test
   class needs `@Autowired` because JUnit creates it, not Spring. The `JdbcClient` bean itself
   comes from Spring Boot's auto-configuration, which builds a `DataSource` from the datasource
   settings and a `JdbcClient` on top of it. Beans are created at startup, so a missing dependency
   fails fast instead of on the first request.

**Spring (exception translation):** `JdbcClient` already turns `SQLException`s into Spring's
`DataAccessException` hierarchy (see the backstop test's `DataIntegrityViolationException`).
For JDBC code, `@Repository` is mostly about bean creation and naming the role.

### `findAll`: the function signature

```kotlin
/** Returns every SKU with its quantity, sorted by SKU id; zero-stock SKUs included, empty list when none. */
fun findAll(): List<InventoryItem> = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory ORDER BY sku_id")
```

**Kotlin:** a function is `fun name(params): ReturnType`. Parameters are written `name: Type`,
the reverse of Java, and the return type comes after the parentheses. `findAll` takes no
parameters. No modifier means `public`, which is what the service needs
([public by default](../../test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)).

`List<InventoryItem>` is a generic type, as in Java. Two Kotlin differences:
- **`List` is read-only.** It has no `add` or `remove`. A changeable list is a `MutableList`. The
  caller gets a snapshot it can't modify.
- **No `?`, so never null.** The compiler won't let this function return `null`. That's how the

**Kotlin (expression body):** `= expression` instead of `{ ... return ... }`. The whole body is one

and `return`, and shortened it once it passed. Concept explained in full in

**SQL:**
- `SELECT sku_id, quantity` names the columns instead of `SELECT *`. The row mapper below reads
  those two columns by name, so the query states exactly what the mapper depends on. A column
  added later can't silently change what the query returns.
- `ORDER BY sku_id`: without `ORDER BY`, SQL guarantees **no** order. Postgres returns rows in

call such as `.list()`.

`(Mutable)List` is Kotlin saying it can't tell whether a Java `List` is meant to be changed. It's

# InventoryItem.kt

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryItem.kt](../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryItem.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-25

## Role

The model: one SKU and how many units of it are in stock. Robert wrote it. It passes through every
layer of `GET /inventory`. The [repository](InventoryRepository.kt.md) builds one per database row,
the [service](InventoryService.kt.md) passes the list through, and the
[controller](InventoryController.kt.md) returns it, where Jackson turns each item into a JSON object.
It is also the shape of the contract's `InventoryItem` schema.

## Walkthrough

### The KDoc and the class

```kotlin
/** One item in the inventory and how much there is of it from the repository for the GET /inventory flow. */

data class InventoryItem(val skuId: String, val quantity: Int)
```

**Kotlin (`data class`):** a `data class` is a class whose job is to hold values. From the
properties in its primary constructor, the compiler generates:

| Generated | What it does | Java equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `equals()` / `hashCode()` | Two items are equal when all their properties are equal | Hand-written, or a Java `record` |
| `toString()` | `InventoryItem(skuId=widget, quantity=5)` | Hand-written, or a `record` |
| `copy(...)` | A new item with some properties changed: `item.copy(quantity = 0)` | No built-in equivalent |
| `component1()`, `component2()` | Destructuring: `val (sku, qty) = item` | Record patterns (Java 21) |

The closest Java equivalent is a `record InventoryItem(String skuId, int quantity)`. Only properties
declared in the primary constructor count toward `equals` and the rest. Value equality is what makes the
repository test work: `assertEquals(listOf(InventoryItem("sold-out", 0)), ...)` compares a list
built in the test with a list built from database rows (see
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](../../test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)).

**Kotlin (`val` in the constructor):** each `val` declares a read-only property and sets it from the
constructor argument, the same way as the
[primary constructor properties](InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection)
in the repository. These two are public (no modifier), because callers and Jackson need to read them.
Robert's first version used `var`. It became `val` because an `InventoryItem` is a **snapshot**
of one row at the moment it was read. Changing `quantity` on the object would change nothing
in the database, and would make the snapshot lie. Stock changes go through a single atomic SQL
statement (see the README decision record), never through a changed object.

**Kotlin (types):** `String` and `Int` have no `?`, so neither can be null. `Int` compiles to
Java's primitive `int`. It would become the boxed `Integer` only if it were nullable (`Int?`) or
used as a generic type argument.

**Kotlin (no body):** the class has no `{ }`, because a data class needs nothing beyond its
constructor. See [class with no body](../InventoryApplication.kt.md).

**Spring (Jackson):** when the controller returns this class, Jackson writes one JSON object per
item, using the property names as keys: `{"skuId": "widget", "quantity": 5}`. So the Kotlin
property names **are** the JSON field names. Renaming `skuId` to `sku` would break the contract.
`jackson-module-kotlin` is what lets Jackson read and build classes like this, which have no no-arg
constructor or setters (see [build.gradle.kts](../../build.gradle.kts.md)).

**Contract:** matches `components.schemas.InventoryItem` in `inventory.yaml`: `skuId` (string) and
`quantity` (integer, `minimum: 0`). The Kotlin type doesn't enforce `minimum: 0`; the database does,
with `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` in [V1__create_inventory.sql](../resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md).

**KDoc placement:** there's a blank line between the KDoc and `data class`. The project's
[check_kdoc.py](../../../../../scripts/check_kdoc.py) treats a blank line as breaking the KDoc's
attachment to the declaration, so it currently reports this class as missing KDoc. That goes on the
review list.

## Check your understanding

- What would `InventoryItem("widget", 5) == InventoryItem("widget", 5)` return? What would it return if `data` were removed?
- Why `val` and not `var`, given that stock quantities change all the time?
- If `skuId` were renamed to `sku`, which test would fail first, and why?

## Role

The model: one SKU and how many units of it are in stock. Robert wrote it. It passes through every
layer of `GET /inventory`. The [repository](InventoryRepository.kt.md) builds one per database row,
the [service](InventoryService.kt.md) passes the list through, and the

It is also the shape of the contract's `InventoryItem` schema.

## Walkthrough

### The KDoc and the class

```kotlin
/** One item in the inventory and how much there is of it from the repository for the GET /inventory flow. */

data class InventoryItem(val skuId: String, val quantity: Int)
```

**Kotlin (`data class`):** a `data class` is a class whose job is to hold values. From the
properties in its primary constructor, the compiler generates:

| Generated | What it does | Java equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `equals()` / `hashCode()` | Two items are equal when all their properties are equal | Hand-written, or a Java `record` |
| `toString()` | `InventoryItem(skuId=widget, quantity=5)` | Hand-written, or a `record` |
| `copy(...)` | A new item with some properties changed: `item.copy(quantity = 0)` | No built-in equivalent |
| `component1()`, `component2()` | Destructuring: `val (sku, qty) = item` | Record patterns (Java 21) |

The closest Java equivalent is a `record InventoryItem(String skuId, int quantity)`. Only properties
declared in the primary constructor count toward `equals` and the rest. Value equality is what makes the
repository test work: `assertEquals(listOf(InventoryItem("sold-out", 0)), ...)` compares a list
built in the test with a list built from database rows (see
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](../../test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)).

constructor argument, the same way as the
[primary constructor properties](InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection)
in the repository. These two are public (no modifier), because callers and Jackson need to read them.
Robert's first version used `var`. It became `val` because an `InventoryItem` is a **snapshot**
of one row at the moment it was read. Changing `quantity` on the object would change nothing
in the database, and would make the snapshot lie. Stock changes go through a single atomic SQL
statement (see the README decision record), never through a changed object.

**Kotlin (types):** `String` and `Int` have no `?`, so neither can be null. `Int` compiles to
Java's primitive `int`. It would become the boxed `Integer` only if it were nullable (`Int?`) or
used as a generic type argument.

constructor. See [class with no body](../InventoryApplication.kt.md).

constructor or setters (see [build.gradle.kts](../../build.gradle.kts.md)).

# InventoryService.kt

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryService.kt](../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryService.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-25

## Role

The service layer, written by Robert. It sits in the middle of the request flow: controller →
**service** → repository. The [controller](InventoryController.kt.md) calls it, and it calls the
[repository](InventoryRepository.kt.md). For `GET /inventory` there are no business rules, so it
passes the repository's list straight through.

## Walkthrough

### Imports

```kotlin
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service
```

**Kotlin:** `InventoryRepository` and `InventoryItem` are in the same package, so they need no
import (see the [repository notes](InventoryRepository.kt.md#imports)).

### A Spring bean that depends on the repository

```kotlin
/** Service class for the get /inventory flow. Use by controller layer and consumes the repository layer. */
@Service
class InventoryService(
    private val inventoryRepository: InventoryRepository
    ){
```

**Kotlin:** a primary constructor with a `private val` property, the same pattern as the
repository's `JdbcClient` (explained in full in
[InventoryRepository.kt](InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection)).
There's no trailing comma after the parameter here. It's optional, so both forms compile.

**Spring:** `@Service` is a stereotype annotation like `@Repository`. It makes component scanning
create an `InventoryService` bean at startup. Spring sees the single constructor, finds the
`InventoryRepository` bean, and passes it in. Startup order follows from that: the repository
bean has to exist before the service can be built, and the service before the controller. If any
bean in that chain were missing, the app would fail at startup, not on the first request.
Functionally `@Service` is the same as `@Component`. It exists to name the class's role.

**Kotlin + Spring:** Kotlin classes are final by default, but the `plugin.spring` compiler plugin
opens classes annotated with `@Service` (and the other stereotypes) so Spring can proxy them later,
for example for `@Transactional` (see [final by default](../../build.gradle.kts.md)).

### `listInventory`

```kotlin
/** Function that returns the list of sorted inventory items. */
fun listInventory() : List<InventoryItem> = inventoryRepository.findAll()
```

**Kotlin:** an [expression body](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean):
the function's result is the value of `inventoryRepository.findAll()`. The declared return type
`List<InventoryItem>` is read-only and non-null, the same type the repository returns (see
[read-only `List`](InventoryRepository.kt.md#findall-the-function-signature)). The space before
the `:` is unusual but legal. Kotlin ignores it.

**Why no error handling:** Robert asked whether this function needs a `try`/`catch`. It doesn't:
- **No data** is not an error. The repository returns an empty list, which becomes `[]`, and the
  contract asks for exactly that.
- **Null** can't happen. The types say `List<InventoryItem>`, not `List<InventoryItem>?`, and
  the compiler enforces it.
- **A database failure** throws Spring's `DataAccessException`, which is unchecked. Kotlin has no
  checked exceptions at all, so there's no `throws` clause to write. The exception travels up
  through the controller, and Spring Boot turns it into a `500` response. Catching it here and
  returning an empty list would be worse: the client would be told "no stock" when the truth is
  "we couldn't look".

Service-layer errors arrive with the purchase endpoint: `404` for a missing SKU, `400` for
insufficient stock.

**Why a service at all, when it only delegates:** the controller could call the repository
directly. The layer is kept because the next endpoints need it: purchase rules ("does the SKU
exist? is there enough stock?") and the mapping of failures to `404`/`400` belong here, not in the
controller (HTTP) or the repository (SQL). Starting the layering now means `GET /inventory` won't
need to be rewired later.

## Check your understanding

- Why is there no `try`/`catch` in `listInventory`? What does the client see if Postgres is down?
- In what order does Spring create the repository, service and controller beans, and why that order?
- What would happen at startup if `@Service` were removed?

# InventoryController.kt

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryController.kt](../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryController.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-25

## Role

The web layer, written by Robert, and the top of the request flow: **controller** → service →
repository. It turns an HTTP request for `GET /inventory` into a call to the
[service](InventoryService.kt.md), and hands the result back to Spring to write as JSON. It holds no
logic of its own. [InventoryControllerTest](../../test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md)
checks it end to end through MockMvc.

## Walkthrough

### Imports

```kotlin
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController
```

**Spring:** all three annotations come from Spring MVC's `web.bind.annotation` package, which is
on the classpath through `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` (see [build.gradle.kts](../../build.gradle.kts.md)).

### A REST controller mapped to `/inventory`

```kotlin
/** Controller for the inventory Flow. At the top layer, the controller layer, and calls the service layer. */
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/inventory")
class InventoryController (
    private val inventoryService: InventoryService
){
```

**Spring (`@RestController`):** this is `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody`, in one annotation.
- `@Controller` is a stereotype, so component scanning makes the class a bean (like `@Service`),
  and Spring MVC scans it for request mappings.
- `@ResponseBody` says "a function's return value **is** the response body". Spring passes it to
  an HTTP message converter, here Jackson, which writes it as JSON.

With only `@Controller`, Spring would treat the return value as the **name of a view** (an HTML
template) to render. There are no templates in this project, so the request would fail. That's why
a JSON API uses `@RestController`.

**Spring (`@RequestMapping` on the class):** sets a base path for every handler in this class.
Each function's mapping is added to the end of it. Robert chose this over putting the full path on
each function. It's the usual Spring pattern, and it will fit the next endpoints: a
`@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` in this class will map to `/inventory/{skuId}`.

**Kotlin:** constructor injection of the service, the same pattern as the
[repository](InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection). The space in
`InventoryController (` is legal and changes nothing.

### The `// Contact:` comment

```kotlin
// Contact: The below mapping maps to the Get /Inventory endpoint in the inventory.yaml contract. The endpoint is a simple and returns all inventory.
```

**Contract:** this line is meant to be the file's `// Contract:` comment (it's spelled `Contact`
at the moment). The part of `inventory.yaml` the function satisfies is `paths./inventory.get`
(`operationId: listInventory`): a `200` with `application/json`, a body that is an array of
`InventoryItem`, and "If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array."

**Placement:** it sits above the KDoc, separated by a blank line, so the KDoc stays directly on top
of the function it documents.

### `GET /inventory`

```kotlin
/** A function that calls inventory service and returns a list of inventory items.*/
@GetMapping
fun findAllInventory(): List<InventoryItem> = inventoryService.listInventory()
```

**Spring (`@GetMapping`):** short for `@RequestMapping(method = [RequestMethod.GET])`. With no
path of its own, it maps to the class's base path, so this function handles `GET /inventory`.
Other methods on that path, such as `DELETE /inventory`, get `405 Method Not Allowed`. Spring
matches paths exactly, and trailing-slash matching has been off by default since Spring 6, so
`GET /inventory/` is a `404`.

The function's **name** doesn't matter to Spring. Only the annotation does. `findAllInventory`,
`list` or `getInventory` would all be routed the same way.

**Spring (what happens after `return`):**
1. The `DispatcherServlet` receives the request and finds this function through its mapping.
2. The function returns a `List<InventoryItem>`.
3. Because of `@ResponseBody`, Spring picks a message converter that can write a list for the
   client's `Accept` header (MockMvc sends none, which means "anything"). Jackson's JSON
   converter matches, so the response gets `Content-Type: application/json`.
4. Jackson writes the list as a JSON array, one object per item, with the Kotlin property
   names as keys ([see InventoryItem](InventoryItem.kt.md)). An empty list becomes `[]`.

The status is `200 OK` because nothing threw and nothing set another status. If the database
fails, the exception passes through here untouched, and Spring Boot's error handling answers `500`
(see [why the service has no try/catch](InventoryService.kt.md#listinventory)).

**Kotlin:** an [expression body](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean)
again. The return type is written out, even though Kotlin could infer it from `listInventory()`.
On a public function that's the better choice: the signature shows what the endpoint returns
without anyone having to look at the service.

**Contract:** returning `List<InventoryItem>` is what makes the body "an array of `InventoryItem`".
The empty-array rule comes from the repository returning an empty list, not from anything here.
`InventoryControllerTest` checks both cases with `JsonCompareMode.STRICT`.

## Check your understanding

- What would the response be if `@RestController` were replaced with `@Controller`?
- Which path does `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` in this class map to, and why?
- What status does `POST /inventory` get today, and what about `GET /inventory/`?
- Where in this code is JSON produced? Which part decides the field names?

-## Role
-The web layer, written by Robert, and the top of the request flow: **controller** → service →
-repository. It turns an HTTP request for `GET /inventory` into a call to the
-[service](InventoryService.kt.md), and hands the result back to Spring to write as JSON. It holds no

-### Imports
-```kotlin
-import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping
-import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping
-import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController
-**Spring:** all three annotations come from Spring MVC's `web.bind.annotation` package, which is
-on the classpath through `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` (see [build.gradle.kts](../../build.gradle.kts.md)).
-### A REST controller mapped to `/inventory`
-```kotlin
-/** Controller for the inventory Flow. At the top layer, the controller layer, and calls the service layer. */
-@RestController
-@RequestMapping("/inventory")
-class InventoryController (
-    private val inventoryService: InventoryService
-**Spring (`@RestController`):** this is `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody`, in one annotation.
-- `@Controller` is a stereotype, so component scanning makes the class a bean (like `@Service`),
-  and Spring MVC scans it for request mappings.
-- `@ResponseBody` says "a function's return value **is** the response body". Spring passes it to
-  an HTTP message converter, here Jackson, which writes it as JSON.
-With only `@Controller`, Spring would treat the return value as the **name of a view** (an HTML
-template) to render. There are no templates in this project, so the request would fail. That's why
-a JSON API uses `@RestController`.

-Each function's mapping is added to the end of it. Robert chose this over putting the full path on
-each function. It's the usual Spring pattern, and it will fit the next endpoints: a
-`@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` in this class will map to `/inventory/{skuId}`.
-**Kotlin:** constructor injection of the service, the same pattern as the
-[repository](InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection). The space in
-`InventoryController (` is legal and changes nothing.

-```kotlin
-// Contact: The below mapping maps to the Get /Inventory endpoint in the inventory.yaml contract. The endpoint is a simple and returns all inventory.
-**Contract:** this line is meant to be the file's `// Contract:` comment (it's spelled `Contact`
-at the moment). The part of `inventory.yaml` the function satisfies is `paths./inventory.get`
-(`operationId: listInventory`): a `200` with `application/json`, a body that is an array of
-`InventoryItem`, and "If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array."
-**Placement:** it sits above the KDoc, separated by a blank line, so the KDoc stays directly on top
-of the function it documents.

-```kotlin
-/** A function that calls inventory service and returns a list of inventory items.*/
-@GetMapping
-fun findAllInventory(): List<InventoryItem> = inventoryService.listInventory()
-**Spring (`@GetMapping`):** short for `@RequestMapping(method = [RequestMethod.GET])`. With no
-path of its own, it maps to the class's base path, so this function handles `GET /inventory`.
-Other methods on that path, such as `DELETE /inventory`, get `405 Method Not Allowed`. Spring
-matches paths exactly, and trailing-slash matching has been off by default since Spring 6, so
-`GET /inventory/` is a `404`.
-The function's **name** doesn't matter to Spring. Only the annotation does. `findAllInventory`,
-`list` or `getInventory` would all be routed the same way.
-**Spring (what happens after `return`):**
-1. The `DispatcherServlet` receives the request and finds this function through its mapping.
-2. The function returns a `List<InventoryItem>`.
-3. Because of `@ResponseBody`, Spring picks a message converter that can write a list for the
-   client's `Accept` header (MockMvc sends none, which means "anything"). Jackson's JSON
-   converter matches, so the response gets `Content-Type: application/json`.

-without anyone having to look at the service.
-**Contract:** returning `List<InventoryItem>` is what makes the body "an array of `InventoryItem`".

+  and Spring MVC scans it for request mappings.
+- `@ResponseBody` says "a function's return value **is** the response body". Spring passes it to
+  an HTTP message converter, here Jackson, which writes it as JSON.
+With only `@Controller`, Spring would try to render an HTML **view** instead of writing the
+body. A returned `String` is taken as the view's name. A returned object, like this list, is put
+in the model for the view to use, and the view name comes from the URL (`inventory`). There is no
+such template in this project, so the request fails with a `500`. That's why a JSON API uses
+`@RestController`.
+**Spring (`@RequestMapping` on the class):** sets a base path for every handler in this class.
+Each function's mapping is added to the end of it. Robert chose this over putting the full path on
+each function. It's the usual Spring pattern, and it will fit the next endpoints: a
+`@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` in this class will map to `/inventory/{skuId}`.
+**Kotlin:** constructor injection of the service, the same pattern as the
+[repository](InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection). The space in
+`InventoryController (` is legal and changes nothing.
+### The `// Contact:` comment
+```kotlin
+// Contact: The below mapping maps to the Get /Inventory endpoint in the inventory.yaml contract. The endpoint is a simple and returns all inventory.
+**Contract:** this line is meant to be the file's `// Contract:` comment (it's spelled `Contact`
+at the moment). The part of `inventory.yaml` the function satisfies is `paths./inventory.get`
+(`operationId: listInventory`): a `200` with `application/json`, a body that is an array of
+`InventoryItem`, and "If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array."
+**Placement:** it sits above the KDoc, separated by a blank line, so the KDoc stays directly on top
+of the function it documents.
+### `GET /inventory`
+```kotlin
+/** A function that calls inventory service and returns a list of inventory items.*/
+@GetMapping
+fun findAllInventory(): List<InventoryItem> = inventoryService.listInventory()
+**Spring (`@GetMapping`):** short for `@RequestMapping(method = [RequestMethod.GET])`. With no
+path of its own, it maps to the class's base path, so this function handles `GET /inventory`.
+A `@GetMapping` also answers `HEAD` (same status and headers, no body), and Spring MVC answers
+`OPTIONS` itself with an `Allow` header. Every other method on that path, such as `POST` or
+`DELETE /inventory`, gets `405 Method Not Allowed`. Spring
+matches paths exactly, and trailing-slash matching has been off by default since Spring 6, so
+`GET /inventory/` is a `404`.
+The function's **name** doesn't matter to Spring. Only the annotation does. `findAllInventory`,
+`list` or `getInventory` would all be routed the same way.
+**Spring (what happens after `return`):**
+1. The `DispatcherServlet` receives the request and finds this function through its mapping.
+2. The function returns a `List<InventoryItem>`.
+3. Because of `@ResponseBody`, Spring picks a message converter that can write a list for the
+   client's `Accept` header (MockMvc sends none, which means "anything"). Jackson's JSON
+   converter matches, so the response gets `Content-Type: application/json`.
+4. Jackson writes the list as a JSON array, one object per item, with the Kotlin property
+   names as keys ([see InventoryItem](InventoryItem.kt.md)). An empty list becomes `[]`.
+The status is `200 OK` because nothing threw and nothing set another status. If the database
+fails, the exception passes through here untouched, and Spring Boot's error handling answers `500`
+(see [why the service has no try/catch](InventoryService.kt.md#listinventory)).
+**Kotlin:** an [expression body](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean)
+again. The return type is written out, even though Kotlin could infer it from `listInventory()`.
+On a public function that's the better choice: the signature shows what the endpoint returns
+without anyone having to look at the service.
+**Contract:** returning `List<InventoryItem>` is what makes the body "an array of `InventoryItem`".
+The empty-array rule comes from the repository returning an empty list, not from anything here.
+`InventoryControllerTest` checks both cases with `JsonCompareMode.STRICT`.

+- What would the response be if `@RestController` were replaced with `@Controller`?
+- Which path does `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` in this class map to, and why?
+- What status does `POST /inventory` get today, and what about `GET /inventory/`?
+- Where in this code is JSON produced? Which part decides the field names?

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

content.text:
The study notes for the model, service and controller are written, and the doc reviewer gave them a PASS on the second round. `check_notes.py` also passes now.

**New notes** in [docs/learning/notes/main/inventory/](docs/learning/notes/main/inventory/):
- [InventoryItem.kt.md](docs/learning/notes/main/inventory/InventoryItem.kt.md): what `data class` generates (compared with a Java `record`), why you switched from `var` to `val` (an item is a snapshot of one row), and how the property names become the JSON field names.
- [InventoryService.kt.md](docs/learning/notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md): `@Service`, the order Spring creates the beans in, and the answer to your question about why there's no `try`/`catch`. It also covers why the layer exists even though it only passes the list through today.
- [InventoryController.kt.md](docs/learning/notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md): `@RestController` compared with `@Controller`, your class-level `@RequestMapping` plus a bare `@GetMapping`, and what happens between your `return` and the JSON response.

**Also updated:**
- [kotlin-concepts.md](docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md): 6 new rows.
- The README endpoint table: `GET /inventory` is now marked implemented.
- [TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md).
- I removed the `.claude/coding-in-progress` marker, so the notes check covers your code again.

**What the reviewer caught.** The main error was in my explanation of what happens with `@Controller` instead of `@RestController`. I had written that the returned list would be treated as the name of an HTML view. Only a returned `String` is. A list goes into the model, and Spring takes the view name from the URL instead. It finds no such template and answers 500. The smaller fixes:
- `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` requests don't get a 405.
- Returning JSON doesn't need `jackson-module-kotlin`. It only matters when JSON is read into a class, which the POST endpoints will do.
- A few links now point to the right section of the note.

**Two fixes in your code for the step 6 review.** The notes quote your code as it is now, so I'll update the quotes after you change it:
1. The comment in the controller says `// Contact:`, which should be `// Contract:`.
2. In `InventoryItem.kt`, there's a blank line between the KDoc and `data class`, and it makes `check_kdoc.py` fail. It reads a blank line as detaching the KDoc from the class, so the checker reports the class as undocumented.

Nothing is committed yet. Proposed message:
```
Add InventoryController and study notes for GET /inventory
```
Or keep this commit for the controller only and commit the notes separately, whichever you'd rather have in the history. Say "review" when you want step 6 started.
